before.approach:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), about 30 miles west of Winthrop and a quarter mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; a day-use fee or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass is required and the small lot fills early. Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the left, marked by a large cairn.

The South Face routes are reached from the CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch, which is a different saddle from the Liberty Bell-Concord col that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. Rather than trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers; higher up, a reasonable climbers' path appears along its left side and is better than fighting up the gully bed. It sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.

You are at the right saddle when Concord is on one side of you and Lexington on the other, and the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges rather than a steep crack system. If you are facing a crack system, you are at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and looking at the North Face.

There is no approach detail specific to South Face Center beyond this shared approach.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail, then up and LEFT into the Concord-Lexington gully rather than the Liberty Bell-Concord one
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft, roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop and a quarter mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook. A day-use fee or Northwest Forest or Interagency pass is required and the small lot fills early. Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the LEFT, marked by a large cairn.

The South Face routes are reached from the CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch, which is a DIFFERENT SADDLE from the Liberty Bell-Concord col that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. Rather than trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers; higher up, a reasonable climbers' path appears along its LEFT side and is better than fighting up the gully bed. It sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.
hazards: Two notches a few hundred feet apart on one ridge, reached by the same path
A gully bed that is better avoided in favour of the path along its left side
Far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col, so less obvious tread
A small trailhead lot that fills early
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE AT THE RIGHT SADDLE WHEN CONCORD IS ON ONE SIDE OF YOU AND LEXINGTON IS ON THE OTHER, AND THE CONCORD WALL IN FRONT OF YOU GIVES ONTO LOW-ANGLE, GRAVELLY LEDGES RATHER THAN A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM. IF YOU ARE FACING A CRACK SYSTEM, YOU ARE AT THE LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD NOTCH AND LOOKING AT THE NORTH FACE.

That is the notch test, and it is the one that matters, because the two saddles are a few hundred feet apart on the same ridge and both are reached from the same trailhead by the same path.

ARRIVAL AT THIS PARTICULAR ROUTE, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM ARRIVAL AT THE NOTCH: LOOKING FROM THE NOTCH, START UP THE OBVIOUS CRACK IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WALL. This route takes the centre of Concord's south face, climbs through a bulge, and continues trending LEFT. Two right-facing corners put you at a TREE right below the summit block.

SO THE COUNT IS: one crack in the middle, one bulge, two right-facing corners, one tree. If your line runs up the edge of the wall rather than its centre, you are on the tower's other south-face route.

WHY THE NOTCH TEST AND THE ROUTE TEST BOTH MENTION CRACKS WITHOUT CONTRADICTING EACH OTHER: at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch a STEEP crack system rises directly in front of you, which is the North Face. At the Concord-Lexington notch the wall reads as low-angle and gravelly overall, and this route's crack is the obvious feature UP THE MIDDLE of that easier-angled wall. Judge the wall first, then the line.

DESCENT: downclimb or make one full double-rope rappel from the summit back to the notch; with a single rope, use two shorter rappels off intermediate anchor stations.

before.approach: Drive Highway 20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), on the south side of the highway about 30 miles west of Winthrop and roughly 0.25 mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; pay the day-use fee or display a Northwest Forest/Interagency pass (the ~20-car lot fills early). Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, then leave the trail on a climber's boot path that breaks off just past a small stream. Follow this path up through slabs, talus, and heather to the base of the gully descending between Liberty Bell and Concord/Lexington Towers, then climb the gully (often snow- or ice-filled into late June) to the notch. The South Face routes are reached from the notch or by working around the tower's east/south side from there.
before.best_season: July through September, once the Liberty-Concord notch/gully has melted out (it commonly holds snow into late June).

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Concord-Lexington notch
approach_variants.notes:
The South Face is reached from the notch between Concord and Lexington, which is a different saddle from the Liberty Bell-Concord notch that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft, about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass) follow the maintained trail until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the left marked by a large cairn.

Instead of trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers. Higher in that gully a reasonable climbers' path appears along its LEFT side; take it rather than fighting up the gully bed. It leads to the Concord-Lexington notch.

This notch is the quieter of the two — it sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.
hazards: loose ground in the Concord-Lexington gully
easy to end up in the Liberty Bell-Concord gully instead — check which two towers flank your notch
no reliable water above the stream near the climbers'-path junction
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You want the Concord-Lexington notch, meaning the saddle with Concord Tower on one side and Lexington Tower on the other. From it, the South Face is on the Concord (north) side, and it begins gently: a class-2 walk across gravelly, slightly down-sloping ledges gets you to the first belay, so if your first move is a hard pull you are on the wrong line. Higher, a roped scramble along the crest brings you to a sandy stance under a thin blade of rock that climbers call the shark fin, and the last pitch goes over that fin onto the summit block, belaying from bolts. The shark fin is the confirming feature — it is unmistakable and there is nothing like it on the North Face side.

The common error is arriving at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch instead. That col has Liberty Bell on its far side, not Lexington, and from there the Concord wall in front of you is the North Face crack system, not walkable ledges.

before.approach: Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), ~30 miles west of Winthrop, ~0.25 mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; day-use fee or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass required. Hike the Blue Lake Trail ~1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climber's boot path breaking off just past a small stream, climbing through slabs/talus/meadow to the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower (often snow-filled and icy into late June, high rockfall risk after snowmelt). From the notch, drop about 50 feet down the gully on the north side of Concord Tower to the start of the two diagonal cracks that mark the route.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then DROP 50 feet down the north side
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft, roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop and about a quarter mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; a day-use fee or Northwest Forest or Interagency pass is required.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climbers' boot path breaking off just past a small stream, climbing through slabs, talus and meadow to the gully between LIBERTY BELL AND CONCORD TOWER. That gully is often snow-filled and icy into late June and carries high rockfall risk after snowmelt.
hazards: An approach gully that is often snow-filled and icy into late June
High rockfall risk in the gully after snowmelt
A 5.8 R grade, so a fall on the wrong ground is consequential
Two notches on one ridge reached by the same path
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE NOTCH, DROP ABOUT 50 FEET DOWN THE GULLY ON THE NORTH SIDE OF CONCORD TOWER TO THE START OF THE TWO DIAGONAL CRACKS THAT MARK THE ROUTE. That is a measured descent and a countable feature: fifty feet down, then TWO cracks running diagonally.

SO THE TEST IS THAT YOU GO DOWN, NOT UP. Every other line off this notch starts at the notch or above it. If you have arrived at the notch and started climbing straight away, you are on the standard North Face or one of its variations, not on this route.

WHICH NOTCH, BECAUSE THE PEAK HAS TWO AND THEY ARE REACHED THE SAME WAY: this is the LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD notch, and the test at the top of the gully is that A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM RISES IN FRONT OF YOU. If instead the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges, you are at the CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch, which serves the tower's south face, and you are on the wrong side of Concord.

COUNTABLE ON THE ROUTE: three pitches at 5.8 R. If you are more than three pitches up and still climbing, you have linked into something else.

DESCENT: the same as the standard North Face. Rappel chains at the summit allow a doubled-rope rappel toward the notch, or downclimb and scramble back to it.

waypoints.name: Blue Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trailhead on SR-20 a half mile past milepost 162; self-issue Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead, about half a mile past milepost 162 and roughly 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass.

waypoints.name: Meadow / climbers' path split
waypoints.note: Leave Blue Lake Trail at a small meadow and cross a small stream; the climbers' path forks left here toward Liberty Bell/Concord Tower.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Blue Lake Trail up through forest and past small tarns and streams as it climbs into the open basin beneath the Liberty Bell group. Shortly after the trail crosses a small stream near a meadow, watch left for the unsigned but well-trodden climbers' path. It is easy to walk straight past, and staying on the main trail delivers you to Blue Lake rather than the towers.

waypoints.name: Gully below the notch
waypoints.note: Talus/scree gully leading to the notch is usually snow-filled and icy until late June, with high rockfall risk (especially party-induced).
waypoints.directions: The climbers' path steepens immediately, working up slabs, talus and heather meadow into the upper Liberty Bowl. From the trailhead to the col is on the order of 1,900-2,000 ft of gain; figure 1.5-2.5 hours depending on how much snow is still in the bowl. Put the helmet on before you start up the gully itself.

waypoints.name: Liberty Bell–Concord Tower notch
waypoints.note: Notch between the two peaks at roughly 7,300 ft; rope up here, the North Face route starts at the top of the notch.
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully about 400 ft to its top. Early in the season an ice axe, and sometimes crampons, earn their weight here; once it is dry it is loose scree and the rock the snow had been holding together comes down easily.

waypoints.name: Pitch 2 crux (5.7 huecos)
waypoints.note: Crux pitch traverses right then climbs straight up on large huecos; most exposed, sustained section of the route.
waypoints.directions: Belay from the notch. The first pitch follows the obvious crack system up about 80-100 ft of well-protected 5.6 to a big ledge dotted with small trees — it is over quickly and is a fair warm-up. From that ledge the line moves right across easy ground before turning straight up.

waypoints.name: Concord Tower summit
waypoints.note: True summit; descend by reversing to the notch and rappelling Beckey Gully on doubled ropes from fixed chains.
waypoints.directions: From the crux belay head left up the crack systems (a #3 takes the good placement), cross two low-angle 5.0 slabs, and finish by bear-hugging a flake onto the small summit block. Angling right after the huecos instead of staying left puts you on a neighboring line rather than Concord's top. The mantle onto the block is awkward enough that most leaders put in one more piece before committing to it.

before.descent_text: Descend by rappelling back down the North Face line itself — do not try to walk off. From the summit, move to the double-bolt rap chains (a short, slightly awkward step/slither over the summit block gets you to the anchor) and make three single-rope rappels with a 60m rope: rappel 1 goes from the summit chains down the upper face; rappel 2 starts from a bolted anchor just below Pitch 3's 5.0 slab section and drops to the bushy, tree-dotted ledge atop Pitch 1; rappel 3 goes from that ledge back to the base of the climb at the notch. All anchors on this line are fixed bolts/chains (no natural gear or v-thread anchors needed). From the base, reverse the approach: descend the gully/climbers' path back through Liberty Bowl to the Blue Lake Trail and out to the trailhead. Note this is distinct from the South Face descent option some parties use when linking Concord with Lexington Tower — that alternate line is only 2 rappels but the first is a full 30m pull requiring the rope's middle mark to be set correctly at the anchor; the direct North Face descent described here is the standard 3-rappel version.

rappel_detail.pull: Set the middle mark carefully if you are running the full double-rope version — parties who combine the top two rappels report it as a full-length pull with nothing spare.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel from the summit down the upper North Face.
rappel_detail.anchor: summit double-bolt chains (a small tree is also reported at the top anchor)
hazards: The move from the summit onto the anchor is short but exposed and clumsy in boots or with a pack on.
This face stays wet after rain and can be icy early and late in the season, and the rappel stances are where that is felt.
rappel_detail.station: Rap chains on the summit, reached from the true summit by a short, awkward step and slither over the top of the summit block; a small tree is reported beside the top anchor as well. On two ropes this becomes one double-rope rappel that reaches the ledge above pitch 1 in a single go, which is why the same descent is described as three rappels by some parties and two by others.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel to the bushy, tree-dotted ledge atop pitch 1.
hazards: The landing ledge is vegetated and the brush catches rope ends on both the throw and the pull.
Slab above the station stays greasy after rain.
rappel_detail.station: Bolted chain anchor on the climbing line just below the 5.0 slab section of pitch 3. The rappel from it drops to the bushy, tree-dotted ledge at the top of pitch 1.

rappel_detail.pull: Pull well out from the notch so the strands come down clear of the brush on the ledge above.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel from the ledge back to the base of the climb at the notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree anchor with webbing (per a Mountaineers trip report: 'webbing on the tree'), not purely bolted as published claims
hazards: A tree or bush anchor rather than fixed hardware — this is the one station on the descent where you may have to build or replace, so carry webbing and a rap ring.
The rappel lands at the notch, which is the top of the loose approach gully every party climbing Liberty Bell and Concord walks up. Anything dislodged goes straight down it.
rappel_detail.station: The station on the bushy pitch-1 ledge, from which the last rappel returns you to the base of the climb at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. Do not plan on this one being fixed hardware: the published claim that the whole line is bolts and chains with no natural gear needed is contradicted by parties on the ground, one of whom recorded rappelling off webbing on the tree here, and another whose anchor at this level was a small bush that held under testing but was plainly not bomber.

before.rappel_count_note: Three single-rope rappels on one 60 m rope is the standard North Face descent and is what these stations describe; parties carrying two ropes combine the top two into one double-rope rappel and reach the notch in two, which is the same line with a different rope setup rather than a different descent. The claim that the whole line is bolts and chains with no natural gear required is not accurate: a Mountaineers party recorded webbing on the tree for part of it, and another reported a bush as the anchor at that level, so carry webbing and a ring. Keep this distinct from the South Face descent used when linking Concord with Lexington — that is a separate two-rappel line of roughly 30 m each with its own bolted mid-face station, and its stations must not be mixed with these.
before.approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20, about 0.5 mile past milepost 162 and 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the well-graded, well-maintained Blue Lake Trail through forest and past small tarns/streams for roughly 1.5-2 miles as it climbs into the open basin below the Liberty Bell group. Watch on your left (south/east side of the trail) for an unsigned but well-trodden climbers' path branching off shortly after the trail crosses a small stream near a meadow — this is easy to miss if you're not looking for it, and is the standard access to the Liberty Bell / Concord Tower massif rather than continuing on to Blue Lake itself. The climbers' path climbs steeply through slabs, talus, and heather meadow into upper 'Liberty Bowl,' gaining roughly 1,900-2,000 ft over about 1.5 miles (figure 1.5-2.5 hours from the trailhead depending on fitness and snow conditions) to reach the gully/notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower (the Liberty Bell-Concord col, roughly 7,400 ft). This entry gully is frequently snow-filled and can stay icy into late June — many early-season parties carry an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) for it. Because the gully's rock is held together by snow much of the season, rockfall risk rises noticeably once the snow melts out, so helmet up before entering it and be mindful of parties above/below. The North Face route begins essentially at the top of this notch.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route walk-in, which is why the two are so often climbed on the same day. Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass; a mile and a half of maintained trail to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream, marked with a large cairn; then the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the bowl below the towers and up the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft.

In the gully, staying climber's left for the lower two thirds and then crossing to climber's right keeps you on the most stable ground.
hazards: loose, heavily trafficked gully below the notch — helmets, and don't queue underneath another party
hollow-sounding flakes on the upper pitches send debris to the notch
no water above the stream at the Trail #727 junction
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route starts AT the top of the notch, on the Concord (south) side — not below it. Stand on the crest of the Liberty Bell-Concord col and turn to face Concord Tower: the first pitch is the crack system running up that wall to a large ledge holding a few small trees, and that ledge is the pitch-one belay and is visible from the notch. The mistake to avoid is dropping 30 feet down the Liberty Bell side to the tree with the ledge running left into a blocky chimney — that is the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell, the other tower, and parties heading for opposite summits share this saddle all day. If your first pitch tops out on a treed ledge you are on Concord; if it starts by walking a small ledge leftward into a chimney you are on Liberty Bell.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same line, but the gully feeding the Liberty Bell-Concord notch holds snow into late June most years and the boot path lower down may still be buried. Ice axe standard, crampons if it has refrozen.

One upside of the early season here: while the gully is snow-filled the rock in it is locked in place, and rockfall gets noticeably worse once it melts out.

SR-20 is closed across Washington Pass every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so this window begins whenever the highway reopens.
hazards: firm snow in the gully with a long runout below
moat between snow and rock at the base
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access until the highway reopens
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow does not move the start — it is still the crack system on the Concord wall rising directly from the crest of the notch to the treed ledge. What snow does is fill the notch, so the col reads as a smooth saddle and the base of the first pitch can sit above a moat. Look up at the tower on the south side of the col for the treed ledge to confirm you are on the right wall before committing.

itinerary.cal: Frequently linked with Liberty Bell's Beckey Route and/or Lexington Tower's North Face for a multi-summit day since all share the same col/notch approach — add roughly 3-4 hrs per extra summit.

days.note: Hike the Blue Lake Trail and climber's path up to the notch, then climb the North Face's three moderate pitches — a crack to a ledge, a run-out section past hollow rock and huecos, and cracks/slabs to the summit. Reverse to the notch and descend the Beckey Gully.

access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) is gated and closed for winter, typically early-to-mid December through mid-April/May depending on snowpack
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.

access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency (America the Beautiful) Pass

overnight_permit.where: This is general Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land outside any wilderness boundary; parties bivy informally at the trailhead or a highway pullout. A Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is needed to park, and no camping is allowed within a quarter mile of Blue Lake itself.

before.bail: Bolted stances exist partway up the route (e.g., P1, P3) allowing retreat with a single rope if needed.

before.descent_text: Same as the standard North Face: rappel chains at the summit allow a doubled-rope rappel toward the notch, or downclimb/scramble back to the notch.
before.rope_note: Single rack to 3 inches, stoppers and slings, on a 70 m rope. Do not rack off the standard North Face's grades: this variation shares the standard route's opening 5.6 crack off the notch, then takes a sustained 5.8 crack that runs hands to off-width to chimney size where the standard line steps right at 5.6-5.7, and rejoins it for a 5.7 arete pitch near the summit. Off the top, the summit chains take a doubled-rope rappel back toward the notch; parties who rappel the south face instead report single-rope raps.

waypoints.name: Blue Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Signed trailhead on SR-20 ~1 mi west of Washington Pass; follow Blue Lake Trail then the climber's path up to the Concord-Lexington gully.

waypoints.name: Concord Tower Summit
waypoints.note: Shared summit for all Concord Tower routes; North Face follows the crack system directly up the face.

before.approach: Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), ~30 miles west of Winthrop, ~0.25 mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; day-use fee or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass required. Hike the Blue Lake Trail ~1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climber's boot path breaking off just past a small stream, up through slabs/talus/meadow to the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower (often snow-filled/icy into late June). Climb the gully to the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower, where this route starts alongside the standard North Face.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Blue Lake Trailhead on SR-20 (~1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, 5,400 ft), via the Blue Lake Trail to the climbers' path
